t:
Section 5 of the Special Olympics Sport and Empowerment Act of 2004 (Public Law 108–406; 118 Stat. 2296) is amended—
    (1) in paragraph (1), by striking all that follows after “3(a),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years;”; 
    (2) in paragraph (2), by striking all that follows after “3(b),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years; and”; and 
    (3) in paragraph (3), by striking all that follows after “3(c),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years.”.

fable.w: This section only amends the authorization of appropriations in the Special Olympics Sport and Empowerment Act of 2004, extending funding to fiscal year 2017 and the four following years. The tempting reading is that a Special Olympics law implies working with a nonprofit, but nothing here requires consultation, comment, hearings, an advisory body, or a right to sue involving any party outside the federal government. It is purely a funding provision.
fable.s: such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years

opus.w: This section only changes funding authorizations: each paragraph now authorizes "such sums as may be necessary" for fiscal year 2017 and the following four years. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, right to sue, or consultation with outsiders. The Special Olympics is a non-federal organization, but naming it in the Act's title, or funding it, does not bring an outside party into a federal decision, and grants are expressly excluded from the definition.
opus.b: Step 1, the tempting reading: the Special Olympics is a non-federal nonprofit, so the section might look like it brings an outside party into the process. It doesn't. The text only changes the authorization-of-appropriations amounts and fiscal years in Section 5 of the Act. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a role in any federal decision. Even if the funds end up going to the Special Olympics as grants, receiving grants is not participation under the definition.

qwen_chat.w: This section solely authorizes appropriations for specific fiscal years. It does not establish any mechanism for consultation, coordination, or participation with entities outside the federal government. The text is purely about funding levels and does not involve public comment, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states or tribes.
qwen_chat.s: Section 5 of the Special Olympics Sport and Empowerment Act of 2004 (Public Law 108–406; 118 Stat. 2296) is amended— (1) in paragraph (1), by striking all that follows after “3(a),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years;”; (2) in paragraph (2), by striking all that follows after “3(b),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years; and”; and (3) in paragraph (3), by striking all that follows after “3(c),” and inserting “such sums as may be necessary for fiscal year 2017 and each of the 4 succeeding fiscal years.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Special Olympics involves non-federal entities, any funding authorization implies participation. However, the text itself only authorizes appropriations and does not describe any process for consulting with or involving outside parties in a decision.
